description:
We are a team of students passionate about technology, engineering, and space exploration. 

We aim to develop KORA — a system that combines satellite radar data from NASA with ground-based sensors to monitor ground movement and potential risks to buildings and infrastructure.

Our team is already formed, but we are always open to exchanging ideas and collaborating with other participants.
summary:
KORA is an infrastructure monitoring system that combines NASA NISAR satellite radar data with ground-based IoT sensors to detect potential risks to buildings and surrounding terrain.

The project uses satellite observations to identify changes in Earth's surface, such as ground displacement and subsidence, while ESP8266-based sensors monitor structural tilt and movement. These complementary data sources are integrated into a web dashboard that visualizes satellite observations and sensor measurements.

By combining large-scale satellite monitoring with local sensor measurements, KORA aims to provide a more comprehensive view of infrastructure conditions and help identify areas that may require further inspection.

Our solution addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by exploring practical applications of NISAR radar data for monitoring surface changes and supporting infrastructure resilience.
details:
KORA is an early-warning system designed to monitor ground movement and potential building stability issues by combining satellite radar observations with measurements from low-cost IoT devices.

How it works

KORA combines two complementary sources of information.

The first is NASA's NISAR satellite data. Our system retrieves Level 2 GUNW interferograms from ASF DAAC using NASA Earthdata. A separate processing pipeline calculates line-of-sight surface displacement and sends the results to our backend. We have tested this pipeline using a real NISAR data granule covering Lviv.

The second source is a ground-based monitoring device mounted directly on a structure. It is built around a Wemos D1 Mini (ESP8266) and includes an MPU6050 accelerometer and gyroscope for measuring structural tilt and movement, a Foxeer M10Q-120 GPS module (u-blox M10) for determining the device's location, and a DHT11 sensor for measuring temperature and humidity.

The device connects to Wi-Fi through a WiFiManager captive portal, allowing network configuration without hardcoding credentials. It transmits JSON measurements to the server over HTTPS, authenticated with a unique API key for each device.

Our FastAPI backend validates incoming data, applies per-device rate limits, calculates tilt from accelerometer readings, and stores measurements in PostgreSQL. Satellite displacement data is submitted through the same API. The backend compares both data sources against defined thresholds and generates alerts using a shared severity classification rule.

The React-based web dashboard displays monitored objects and their locations on an interactive map, together with alerts, sensor measurements, and tilt history.

Data visualization and external sources

The dashboard combines several geospatial data sources, including NASA GIBS for satellite imagery and NISAR-related map layers, NASA COOLR for reported landslide events, NASA Global Landslide Susceptibility for regional landslide risk context, and OpenStreetMap and Esri basemaps for geographic reference.

Benefits and intended impact

KORA aims to make infrastructure monitoring more accessible and affordable. Satellite radar provides a wide-area perspective, helping identify gradual surface displacement, while locally installed sensors provide frequent measurements at individual structures.

This combination could be particularly useful for buildings and slopes in landslide-prone areas, where changes in ground conditions may require closer inspection. By bringing these observations together in one dashboard, KORA helps users identify unusual changes and prioritize locations for further investigation.

Alerts are intended as early-warning signals that a site may need inspection. They do not determine whether a building is structurally safe or unsafe.

Technologies and tools

We used ESP8266 (Wemos D1 Mini), MPU6050, Foxeer M10Q-120 GPS, and DHT11 for the hardware prototype. The firmware was developed using PlatformIO and Arduino C++.

The backend was developed with Python, FastAPI, and SQLAlchemy, with PostgreSQL for data storage and Render for hosting. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet, and Recharts, and is hosted on Vercel.

For satellite data processing, we used NASA NISAR Level 2 GUNW products, ASF DAAC, and NASA Earthdata. The mapping component integrates NASA GIBS, NASA COOLR, NASA Global Landslide Susceptibility, OpenStreetMap, and Esri basemaps.

We also used the Claude AI assistant by Anthropic to help develop code, tests, and documentation.

Creativity and design considerations

The main creative aspect of KORA is the integration of satellite-based surface displacement measurements with an affordable sensor installed directly on a structure. Instead of relying on a single monitoring method, the system combines a regional view from space with localized measurements from the ground.

During development, we considered affordability, scalability, data security, and reliability. Each device uses an individual API key, stored securely on the server in hashed form, and requests are rate-limited to prevent excessive submissions. We also use a shared severity classification rule to make alert levels consistent and help reduce false alarms.

We recognize the limitations of the available data. NISAR Level 2 products are provisional, and their spatial resolution is approximately 80 meters. Satellite observations indicate changes in the Earth's surface, not cracks or damage inside individual buildings. KORA therefore presents satellite and sensor measurements as complementary indicators that can help identify locations requiring further inspection.
